ai.definition: Regulatory technology (RegTech) for financial compliance is a set of tools and services designed to help financial institutions meet regulatory requirements and manage associated risks by leveraging automation and data analytics.
ai.howItWorks: RegTech solutions typically integrate with existing systems, such as accounting software or CRM platforms. They monitor regulatory updates in real-time, flag potential non-compliance issues, and provide automated reports to ensure ongoing adherence to regulatory standards.
ai.problemSolved: The primary problem RegTech addresses is the complexity and ever-changing nature of financial regulations that can lead to significant operational costs and legal risks for financial institutions if not properly managed.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing in this context refers to the development and deployment of software solutions, which involves coding, testing, and integration with existing IT infrastructure.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes requirements gathering, design, development, testing, and deployment. It often requires collaboration between regulatory experts, software developers, and legal advisors to ensure that the solution accurately reflects current regulations.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include initial setup costs for integration with existing systems, ongoing maintenance and updates as regulations change, and training costs for staff who will use the technology.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: RegTech is expected to continue growing as regulatory requirements become more complex and institutions seek ways to reduce operational risk and cost through automation.
ai.regulation: RegTech solutions must comply with various financial regulations, including those set by central banks, securities exchanges, and other regulatory bodies. Compliance with these regulations can be a significant barrier to entry for new players in the market.
ai.risks: Risks include data privacy concerns, potential inaccuracies or omissions in automated systems, and the need for continuous updates as regulations evolve.
ai.profitability: Profitability is driven by subscription fees, one-time implementation costs, and reduced operational costs from improved compliance. However, the market is highly competitive, and cost pressures can limit profitability.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development trends may include increased use of artificial intelligence for predictive analytics, enhanced integration with blockchain technologies for transparency, and greater focus on user experience to improve adoption rates.

glossary.def: Short for regulatory technology, it refers to the use of software solutions to help financial institutions comply with regulations and manage risks.
The act of adhering to laws, rules, or standards set by regulatory bodies. In finance, this often involves ensuring that business practices meet legal requirements.

subsystems.name: Regulatory intelligence
subsystems.role: Tracks and interprets regulatory changes from official sources.
parts: web crawlers and APIs to official journals

subsystems.name: Data integration
subsystems.role: Pulls and normalises data from core banking, trading and communication systems.

subsystems.name: Analytics and detection
subsystems.role: Flags suspicious activity, risk and anomalies.

subsystems.name: Case management and workflow
subsystems.role: Routes alerts to investigators and records decisions.

subsystems.name: Governance and explainability
subsystems.role: Ensures models and rules are auditable and fair.

buildSteps.title: Map obligations
buildSteps.detail: Legal and compliance analysts break a regulation into concrete, testable requirements.

buildSteps.title: Model the data
buildSteps.detail: Engineers define which internal systems hold the needed data and build pipelines to extract, clean and link it.

buildSteps.title: Encode rules
buildSteps.detail: Requirements are translated into machine-executable rules, often in a domain-specific language, with version control.

buildSteps.title: Train detection models
buildSteps.detail: For risk and AML use cases, historical data and expert labels train and validate machine-learning models.

buildSteps.title: Integrate workflows
buildSteps.detail: Alerts, case management and reporting are wired into daily operations so staff act on the output.

buildSteps.title: Validate and test
buildSteps.detail: Backtesting, model validation and controlled pilots check that the system meets regulatory expectations.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and monitor
buildSteps.detail: The system runs in production with continuous monitoring for model drift, false positives and regulatory change.

buildSteps.title: Update continuously
buildSteps.detail: Horizon scanning feeds new rules and model retraining as regulations evolve.

prerequisites.why: compliance systems must process millions of transactions and communications per day.
general NLP is mature, but reliably interpreting legal text across jurisdictions is still developing.
some regulators publish structured rulebooks, but most rules remain human-readable documents.
the Legal Entity Identifier (LEI, ISO 17442) lets systems link parties across datasets.
regulators require reasons for decisions, and explainability tools are still maturing.
industry-wide utilities need to share risk signals without exposing customer data.

pathway.milestone: rule-based and basic analytics deployed in banks
pathway.unlocks: lower reporting cost and faster detection of obvious breaches.

pathway.milestone: AI and NLP that interpret regulatory change and reduce false positives
pathway.unlocks: proactive compliance and less manual review.

pathway.milestone: shared industry utilities for KYC and AML checks
pathway.unlocks: network effects that make each institution's checks cheaper and more accurate.

pathway.milestone: real-time embedded compliance and supervisory technology (SupTech) used by regulators
pathway.unlocks: continuous supervision and lower systemic risk.
